name: Gregorio Allegri
bio:
Allegri was born in Rome around 1582 and grew up there as a choirboy at San Luigi dei Francesi, the church of the French community, where he studied with the composer Giovanni Bernardino Nanino. He was intended for the Church, and for some years he held a post at the cathedral of Fermo, in central Italy, where he wrote many motets and other sacred works.

His music came to the notice of Pope Urban VIII, and on 6 December 1629 Allegri joined the choir of the Sistine Chapel as a singer, a post he held for the rest of his life. He published collections of sacred concertos and motets, and wrote masses, settings of the Lamentations of Jeremiah and a little music for strings; one of these pieces was printed by the scholar Athanasius Kircher in his great book on music, *Musurgia universalis* (1650). He was remembered as a kind man who gave generously to the poor and to prisoners.

He died in Rome in February 1652. His fame rests almost entirely on one work, the *Miserere*, written in the 1630s for the Holy Week services of the Sistine Chapel. For generations the papal singers performed it with ornaments of their own, passed on by ear, and the music gained an aura of secrecy. The story that the fourteen-year-old Mozart wrote it down from memory in 1770 made it famous across Europe, and 20th-century recordings turned its soaring soprano line into one of the best-known sounds in choral music.

name: Johann Sebastian Bach

facts.label: symphonies
facts.value: None (the form came after his time)

bio:
Bach was born in Eisenach in 1685, the youngest child of a town musician, into a family that had produced musicians for generations. Orphaned at ten, he lived for five years with his eldest brother, an organist, and went on to work as an organist himself in Arnstadt and Mühlhausen and then at the court of Weimar, where he became known above all as a brilliant player.

In 1717 he became music director to Prince Leopold of Anhalt-Köthen, a keen musician who paid him well. The Calvinist court needed little church music, so Bach wrote instrumental works there, among them the *Brandenburg Concertos*. In 1723 he moved to Leipzig as Thomaskantor, responsible for the music of the city’s main churches and the St Thomas School, and held the post for 27 years. There he wrote whole yearly cycles of church cantatas, the *St Matthew Passion* and, later, the *Mass in B minor*.

He had twenty children, four of whom became composers. After his death in 1750 he was remembered mainly as an organist, and his music was thought old-fashioned. Mendelssohn’s performance of the *St Matthew Passion* in 1829 started a revival that has never stopped. His mastery of [[fugue|fugue]] and of weaving several melodies together is now seen as one of the foundations of Western music.
birthdayNote: In 1705 Bach travelled about 450 km from Arnstadt to Lübeck, reportedly on foot, to hear the organist Dieterich Buxtehude, and stayed some three months longer than the leave allowed.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1685 (Old Style), in Eisenach.

name: Samuel Barber

facts.label: bestKnownFor
facts.value: *Adagio for Strings*, *Knoxville: Summer of 1915*, the opera *Vanessa*

bio:
Barber was born in 1910 in West Chester, Pennsylvania, the son of a doctor. Music ran in the family: his aunt, Louise Homer, was a leading contralto at the Metropolitan Opera, and her husband, the songwriter Sidney Homer, guided him for more than twenty-five years. He wrote his first piece at seven, and at nine left his mother a note: he was not meant to be an athlete but a composer. At fourteen he entered the new Curtis Institute of Music in Philadelphia, where he studied composition, piano and singing, and where in 1928 he met the Italian composer Gian Carlo Menotti, his partner for more than forty years.

Success came early. For a while he also sang professionally as a baritone, on NBC radio. A Rome Prize took him to Italy, where he wrote his Symphony in One Movement, and in 1938 Arturo Toscanini conducted his *Adagio for Strings* on the radio, making him famous. His music stayed lyrical and largely tonal while much modern music turned away from melody. He served in the Army Air Corps during the Second World War, and from 1943 he and Menotti lived at Capricorn, a house north of New York, where he wrote much of his best music, including *Knoxville: Summer of 1915* for soprano and orchestra.

He won the Pulitzer Prize twice, for his opera *Vanessa* (1958) and for his Piano Concerto, written for the opening of Lincoln Center in New York. His opera *Antony and Cleopatra*, which opened the new Metropolitan Opera House in 1966, was poorly received, and in his last years he struggled with depression and drinking and wrote less. He died of cancer in New York on 23 January 1981, aged 70, and was buried in his home town of West Chester.
birthdayNote: The *Adagio for Strings* began as the slow movement of a string quartet, written in 1936 when Barber was 26. Two years later Toscanini conducted it on the radio, and it has hardly been silent since.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1910, in West Chester.

name: Béla Bartók

facts.label: born
facts.value: 25 March 1881, Nagyszentmiklós, Hungary (now Sânnicolau Mare, Romania)

facts.label: symphonies
facts.value: None numbered; the *Concerto for Orchestra* fills the role

facts.label: bestKnownFor
facts.value: *Concerto for Orchestra*, six string quartets, *Music for Strings, Percussion and Celesta*

bio:
Bartók was born in 1881 in Nagyszentmiklós, then in Hungary and now in Romania. His father, the director of an agricultural school, died when he was seven, and his mother moved the family several times before settling in Pozsony (now Bratislava). He gave his first public recital at eleven and from 1899 to 1903 studied the piano and composition at the Academy of Music in Budapest, where he met Zoltán Kodály. His early works, such as the symphonic poem *Kossuth* (1903), were written in a late-Romantic style.

In 1904 he heard a young woman, Lidi Dósa, singing folk songs, and soon he and Kodály were travelling from village to village, collecting Hungarian, Slovak and Romanian songs, many of them with a phonograph; later he collected in Algeria (1913) and Turkey (1936). The old peasant tunes, with their unusual modes and irregular rhythms, transformed his own music. From 1907 to 1934 he taught the piano at the Budapest Academy. He wrote the opera *Duke Bluebeard’s Castle* (1911), the ballets *The Wooden Prince* and *The Miraculous Mandarin*, six string quartets, *Music for Strings, Percussion and Celesta* (1936) and *Mikrokosmos*, a cycle of piano pieces written partly for his son Péter.

As Hungary drew closer to Nazi Germany, he emigrated to the United States in October 1940 with his second wife, the pianist Ditta Pásztory. Life there was hard: little money, few performances and, from 1943, the leukaemia that would kill him. A commission from Serge Koussevitzky led to the *Concerto for Orchestra* (1943), his most popular work. He died in New York on 26 September 1945, leaving his Third Piano Concerto almost finished and a Viola Concerto in sketches. In 1988 his remains were brought back to Budapest and reburied after a state funeral.
birthdayNote: In November 1936 Bartók travelled to southern Turkey to record folk songs. With Ahmed Adnan Saygun and two young Ankara teachers, Ulvi Cemal Erkin and Necil Kazım Akses, he went from village to village around Osmaniye.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1881, in Nagyszentmiklós.

name: Ludwig van Beethoven
bio:
Beethoven grew up in Bonn, in a family of court musicians. His father, a singer, pushed him hard as a child prodigy, and in his teens Ludwig was already playing in the court orchestra and helping to support the family. In 1792 he moved to Vienna to study with Haydn, and he soon made his name there as a ferocious pianist, famous above all for his improvising.

In his late twenties he began to lose his hearing. In 1802, in a letter to his brothers now known as the Heiligenstadt Testament, he admitted that he had thought of ending his life, and that only his art had held him back. What followed was a burst of bold, large-scale works, among them the *Eroica* and the Fifth Symphony. By his last years he was almost completely deaf, yet he kept composing, and wrote the Ninth Symphony and his late string quartets.

Beethoven died in Vienna in 1827, and a huge crowd followed his funeral procession. He changed what people expected music to do: a symphony could now be a personal statement, a struggle that ends in triumph, or a deep meditation. He stretched old forms such as [[sonata-form|sonata form]] until they could hold far more drama than before. Almost every composer who came after him, from Brahms to Mahler, worked in his shadow.
birthdayNote: Only the baptism was recorded, in Bonn on 17 December 1770, so this is Beethoven’s day. Posters for the first public concert, in 1778, gave the young performer’s age as six. The real age was seven.
birthdayLine: Baptised on this day in 1770, in Bonn.

name: Hector Berlioz
bio:
Berlioz was born in 1803 in La Côte-Saint-André, a small town near Grenoble, where his father was a doctor. He was sent to Paris to study medicine, but he hated the dissecting room and spent his evenings at the opera instead. Against his family’s wishes he gave up medicine for music and entered the Paris Conservatoire. Unusually for a composer, he never became a real pianist; his instruments were the flute and the guitar.

In 1827 he saw the Irish actress Harriet Smithson play Ophelia and Juliet, and fell obsessively in love with her. That passion poured into the *Symphonie fantastique* of 1830, a piece of [[programme-music|programme music]] about an artist’s love, his opium dreams and a nightmarish witches’ sabbath, with the beloved represented by a returning melody, the [[idee-fixe|idée fixe]]. He did eventually meet and marry Harriet, but the marriage was unhappy.

Berlioz thought in sound and colour, and his book on orchestration was studied by composers for generations. In France he was often misunderstood and made much of his living as a music critic, while audiences in Germany, Russia and England welcomed him as a conductor. His epic opera *Les Troyens* was never staged complete in his lifetime. He died in Paris in 1869.
birthdayNote: Berlioz was 26 when the *Symphonie fantastique* was written: a love story told with harps, church bells and a witches’ dance on the old *Dies irae* chant. Nearly two centuries on, it still sounds wild.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1803, in La Côte-Saint-André.

name: Georges Bizet

facts.label: symphonies
facts.value: One, the Symphony in C, and the symphony *Roma*

bio:
Bizet was born in Paris in 1838. He was registered as Alexandre César Léopold but baptised Georges, the name he kept. His father, a former wigmaker, had become a singing teacher, and his mother was a fine pianist. The boy was so gifted that the Paris Conservatoire took him at nine, below the official age. He won first prize for piano, studied composition with Fromental Halévy and became a friend of the young Camille Saint-Saëns. At seventeen he wrote a Symphony in C full of youthful sparkle, but never published it; it was found again in 1933 and first played in 1935.

In 1857 he won the Prix de Rome and spent nearly three years at the Villa Medici in Rome. Back in Paris, success would not come. The opera houses preferred established names, and he earned his living largely by arranging other composers’ music. Neither *The Pearl Fishers* (1863) nor *The Fair Maid of Perth* (1867) succeeded at first. In 1869 he married Geneviève Halévy, his late teacher’s daughter; their only son, Jacques, was born in 1872. That year his music for Alphonse Daudet’s play *L’Arlésienne* failed in the theatre, but the concert suite he made from it was an immediate success.

His last opera, *Carmen*, opened at the Opéra-Comique on 3 March 1875, the day his appointment to the Legion of Honour was announced. Its realism and its heroine, who lives and dies by her own rules, shocked the audience, and Bizet believed it had failed. Three months later, on 3 June 1875, his sixth wedding anniversary, he died of a heart attack at Bougival, near Paris, aged 36. Within a few years *Carmen* was being performed all over the world, and it is now one of the most popular operas ever written.
birthdayNote: The Habanera in *Carmen* borrows a tune by the Spanish composer Sebastián Yradier. Bizet took it for a folk song, and added a credit to the score once the truth came out.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1838, in Paris.

name: Alexander Borodin

facts.label: bestKnownFor
facts.value: *Prince Igor*, *In the Steppes of Central Asia*, String Quartet No. 2

bio:
Borodin was born in St Petersburg in 1833, the illegitimate son of an elderly Georgian nobleman, Luka Gedevanishvili. The nobleman registered the boy as the son of one of his serfs, Porfiry Borodin, which is where the name comes from, and freed him when he was seven. Taught at home by private tutors, he entered the Medical–Surgical Academy in St Petersburg in 1850 and became a chemist. From 1859 he worked for three years in Heidelberg, where he played chamber music on the cello and met the pianist Ekaterina Protopopova, whom he married in 1863.

In 1862 he became professor of chemistry at the Medical–Surgical Academy, a career he kept all his life. He is credited, with the Frenchman Charles-Adolphe Wurtz, with discovering the aldol reaction, and he helped to found medical courses for women. In the same year he began lessons with Mily Balakirev and joined the circle later known as The Five, who wanted music that sounded Russian. He composed in the time his work left him, often when he was ill: the First Symphony was first played in 1869, the Second in 1877, and the orchestral picture *In the Steppes of Central Asia* followed in 1880. That year Liszt arranged a performance of the First Symphony in Germany.

His great project was the opera *Prince Igor*, which occupied him from the late 1860s until his death; Rimsky-Korsakov and Glazunov completed it. Its Polovtsian Dances are his best-known music. He died suddenly at a ball in St Petersburg in February 1887, aged 53. His long, lyrical melodies and rich harmonies later fascinated Debussy and Ravel, and in 1953 Broadway turned them into the musical *Kismet*.
birthdayNote: A professor of chemistry all along, Borodin took up the name “Sunday composer”, writing music when the laboratory allowed. The String Quartet No. 2 shows what those Sundays could hold.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1833, in St Petersburg.

name: Johannes Brahms
bio:
Brahms was born in Hamburg in 1833, the son of a double-bass player who scraped a living in the city’s dance halls and theatres. Johannes was earning money at the piano while still a teenager. In 1853 he met Robert and Clara Schumann, and Robert, then one of the most respected composers in Germany, published an article hailing the twenty-year-old as the future of music.

Schumann’s praise was both a gift and a burden. Brahms worked on his First Symphony for about twenty years, all too aware of Beethoven looking over his shoulder, and it was finally premiered in 1876, when he was 43. After Robert Schumann’s death he remained devoted to Clara for the rest of her life, as friend and confidant; the exact nature of their bond is still debated.

He settled in Vienna in the 1860s and became one of the most admired figures in European music, writing four symphonies, *A German Requiem*, concertos, and a great deal of chamber music and songs. Brahms loved old forms such as the [[variation|variation]] and the [[passacaglia|passacaglia]], and filled them with warm, autumnal feeling. He died in Vienna in 1897, less than a year after Clara.
birthdayNote: The famous Brahms lullaby was a present, written in 1868 for a friend’s new baby. Today Brahms shares a birthday with Tchaikovsky, born seven years later.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1833, in Hamburg.

name: Max Bruch
bio:
Bruch was born in Cologne in 1838. His mother, Wilhelmine, was a singer, and his father a lawyer who rose to be deputy head of the city’s police. He had his early training from the composer Ferdinand Hiller, and his talent was noticed by the pianist Ignaz Moscheles. Bruch spent the first half of his career moving from post to post as a conductor and choral director: Mannheim, Koblenz, where he wrote the first version of his First Violin Concerto, Sondershausen, Berlin and Bonn.

In his own time he was known above all for large choral works, such as *Odysseus*. Like his contemporary Brahms, he stood for the classical tradition against the “New Music” of Liszt and Wagner. From 1880 to 1883 he conducted the Liverpool Philharmonic Society, and in 1881 he married the singer Clara Tuczek. Besides the First Violin Concerto, his best-known works are the *Scottish Fantasy* for violin and orchestra and *Kol Nidrei* for cello and orchestra, based on a Jewish melody. From 1890 to 1910 he taught composition in Berlin; Ottorino Respighi was one of his pupils.

He wrote three violin concertos and three symphonies, but the First Violin Concerto eclipsed everything else, which exasperated him. Because of *Kol Nidrei*, many assumed he was Jewish. He was a Protestant, but under the Nazis his music was restricted and largely forgotten in Germany. After the First World War he was left poor, and he died in Berlin in 1920. His gravestone reads “Music is the language of God”.
birthdayNote: Bruch sold the First Violin Concerto outright and earned nothing from its huge later success, a lasting grievance. Violinists, and listeners, have been grateful for it ever since.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1838, in Cologne.

name: Anton Bruckner

facts.label: symphonies
facts.value: Nine numbered (the Ninth unfinished), plus two early ones

bio:
Bruckner was born in 1824 in Ansfelden, a village near Linz in Upper Austria, the eldest child of the village schoolmaster. His father gave him his first music lessons and taught him the organ. When his father died in 1837, the 13-year-old was sent to the Augustinian monastery of St Florian as a choirboy, and he was in awe of its great organ. He trained as a schoolteacher and spent his late teens and twenties teaching in village schools, playing the organ and composing on the side.

In 1848 he became organist at St Florian, and in 1855 he won the post of cathedral organist in Linz. That same year he began years of study, mostly by post, with the Viennese theorist Simon Sechter. He only started composing in earnest at 37, after lessons with the young conductor Otto Kitzler, who introduced him to the music of Richard Wagner. In 1868 he moved to Vienna to teach at the Conservatory, and as an organist he toured France in 1869 and England in 1871, where he played at the Royal Albert Hall.

His symphonies had a hard time in Vienna. Bruckner revered Wagner and dedicated his Third Symphony to him, and from then on the city’s most powerful critic, Eduard Hanslick, a champion of Brahms, treated him as a dangerous Wagnerite. The Third’s premiere in 1877 was a fiasco. Real success came only at 60, with the Seventh Symphony in Leipzig in 1884. Fiercely self-critical, he revised his scores again and again, which is why many exist in several versions. He died in Vienna in 1896 with his Ninth Symphony unfinished, and lies in the crypt of St Florian, beneath his favourite organ.
birthdayNote: Bruckner is said to have dedicated the Ninth Symphony “to the beloved God”. Its slow third movement, which ends in peace, was the last movement Bruckner completed.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1824, in Ansfelden.

name: Frédéric Chopin

facts.label: bestKnownFor
facts.value: Piano music: nocturnes, ballades, études, mazurkas, polonaises

bio:
Chopin was born in 1810 in Żelazowa Wola, a village west of Warsaw, to a French father, Nicolas, who had settled in Poland, and a Polish mother. The family moved to Warsaw when he was a baby, and Polish was spoken at home. He was giving public concerts by the age of seven, and from 1826 he studied composition with Józef Elsner at the Warsaw Conservatory. In November 1830 he left to make his name abroad. A few weeks later the November Uprising broke out at home, and he never saw Poland again.

He reached Paris in 1831 and stayed for the rest of his life. He disliked large halls and gave only about thirty public concerts; he earned his living by teaching and played mostly in private salons. In 1836 he met the novelist George Sand. They were together from 1838 to 1847, spending a difficult winter on Mallorca and most summers at her country house at Nohant, where he wrote many of his finest works.

Almost everything he wrote involves the piano: nocturnes, études, ballades, preludes, scherzos, and the Polish dances, mazurkas and polonaises, that kept his homeland in his music. Often ill, he gave his last Paris concert in February 1848 and toured Britain that year. He died in Paris on 17 October 1849, aged 39, and the funeral march from his Second Piano Sonata was played at his graveside.
birthdayNote: The Chopin family kept this day, though the parish register says 22 February. At 20, Chopin played the E minor Piano Concerto at a farewell concert in Warsaw, weeks before leaving Poland for good.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1810, in Żelazowa Wola.

name: Arcangelo Corelli

facts.label: symphonies
facts.value: None (the form came after his time)

facts.label: bestKnownFor
facts.value: *Christmas Concerto*, concerti grossi Op. 6, violin sonatas Op. 5 (with *La Folia*)

bio:
Corelli was born in 1653 in Fusignano, a small town in Romagna, then part of the Papal States; his father had died five weeks before. He had his first music lessons in nearby towns and in 1666 moved to Bologna, a city with a famous school of violinists, and the title pages of his first three published collections still call him “il Bolognese”. Many stories about his youth, such as a trip to Paris from which the jealous Lully is said to have chased him, are legends without contemporary evidence.

By 1675 he was playing in Rome, which became his home. The city had no permanent orchestra, but its cardinals and princes staged lavish performances, and Corelli became the man who led them, sometimes with more than a hundred players. He directed music for Queen Christina of Sweden, worked for Cardinal Benedetto Pamphili and then for Cardinal Pietro Ottoboni, in whose palace he lived and led celebrated Monday concerts. He was admired as a violinist and as a strict leader who wanted every bow in the orchestra to move together.

He published little: five sets of sonatas between 1681 and 1700, the last of them, Op. 5, ending with variations on *La Folia*, and the twelve concertos of Op. 6, each a [[concerto-grosso|concerto grosso]], which appeared in Amsterdam in 1714. They became models for a whole generation; Handel, Vivaldi, Bach and Couperin all learned from them, and Bach based an organ fugue on one of his themes. Corelli died in Rome on 8 January 1713, a wealthy man with a collection of paintings and fine violins, and was buried in the Pantheon.
birthdayNote: Corelli wanted a whole orchestra to bow as one, all up or all down. Francesco Geminiani, probably his pupil, said he would stop a rehearsal if he saw a single bow out of line.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1653, in Fusignano.

name: Claude Debussy

facts.label: bestKnownFor
facts.value: *Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune*, *La mer*, piano music

bio:
Debussy was born in 1862 in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, outside Paris, into a family of modest means with little interest in the arts. His talent at the piano won him a place at the Paris Conservatoire at the age of ten. There he discovered that he cared more about inventing new harmonies than about following the rules, which his teachers did not appreciate. All the same, in 1884 he won the Prix de Rome, France’s most prestigious prize for young composers, and spent two unhappy years at the Villa Medici in Rome.

Back in Paris he fell under Wagner’s spell, travelling to Bayreuth in 1888 and 1889, and then worked hard to free himself from it. At the 1889 World’s Fair in Paris he heard a Javanese gamelan orchestra, whose shimmering sounds and scales stayed with him. His *Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune* (1894) opened a new chapter in music; Pierre Boulez later said that modern music was awakened by it. Fame came in 1902, when he was nearly forty, with his only completed opera, *Pelléas et Mélisande*.

His private life caused a scandal in 1904, when he left his wife for Emma Bardac; their daughter, Claude-Emma, known as Chouchou, was born in 1905, the year of *La mer*. He went on to write the orchestral *Images* and two books of piano *Préludes*, and he always rejected the label “Impressionist”. He died of cancer in Paris on 25 March 1918, while the city was under German bombardment.
birthdayNote: Debussy asked for Hokusai’s *Great Wave* on the cover of the first edition of *La mer*. Much of the music was begun far from any coast, inland in Burgundy.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1862, in Saint-Germain-en-Laye.

name: Paul Dukas
bio:
Dukas was born in Paris in 1865 into a Jewish family. His father was a banker; his mother, a pianist, died when he was five. He entered the Paris Conservatoire at the end of 1881 and studied composition with Ernest Guiraud; Claude Debussy, a fellow student, became a close friend. In 1888 he came second in the Prix de Rome with his cantata *Velléda*, and the next year he left the Conservatoire.

From 1892 he earned a name as a music critic, writing regularly for at least five French journals, and with Camille Saint-Saëns he worked on a new edition of the music of Rameau. His own works appeared slowly: the overture *Polyeucte* (1891), a Symphony in C (1895–96) and, in 1897, the [[scherzo|scherzo]] *The Sorcerer’s Apprentice*, after a ballad by Goethe. It became so popular that it overshadowed everything else he wrote, which irritated him. His opera *Ariane et Barbe-bleue*, on a text by Maurice Maeterlinck, was staged at the Opéra-Comique in 1907, and the ballet *La Péri* followed in 1912.

*La Péri* was his last large work. Dukas was fiercely self-critical and destroyed many of his compositions; after 1912 he finished only a few short pieces, among them a tribute to Debussy in 1920. He became an influential teacher instead: from 1927 he taught composition at the Conservatoire and at the École Normale de Musique, and his pupils included Olivier Messiaen, Maurice Duruflé and Joaquín Rodrigo. He was elected to the Académie des Beaux-Arts in 1934 and died in Paris on 17 May 1935, aged 69.
birthdayNote: Dukas was so hard on his own music that he destroyed many of his manuscripts. *The Sorcerer’s Apprentice* survived, and became so popular that it came to irritate him.

name: Antonín Dvořák
bio:
Dvořák was born in 1841 in Nelahozeves, a village on the Vltava north of Prague, where his father was a butcher and innkeeper. He was expected to take over the family business, but music won. He studied at the organ school in Prague, then spent years playing the viola in a theatre orchestra, which for a time was conducted by Bedřich Smetana.

Recognition came in his thirties. Brahms sat on the jury that awarded him an Austrian state grant, and he recommended Dvořák to his own publisher, Simrock, who brought out the *Slavonic Dances* in 1878 to huge success. Dvořák’s music, full of the dance rhythms and melodies of Bohemia and Moravia, made him famous across Europe, and especially in England, which he visited nine times.

In 1892 he went to New York as director of the National Conservatory of Music. There he wrote his Ninth Symphony, *From the New World*, and spent a summer among the Czech community of Spillville, Iowa. Homesick, he returned to Bohemia in 1895, later became director of the Prague Conservatory, and wrote his opera *Rusalka*. He died in Prague in 1904.
birthdayNote: Dvořák loved trains all life long and is quoted as saying, “I’d give all my symphonies if I could have invented the locomotive.” Luckily for us, nobody took up the offer.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1841, in Nelahozeves.

name: Edward Elgar

facts.label: symphonies
facts.value: Two (a third completed from his sketches by Anthony Payne)

facts.label: bestKnownFor
facts.value: *Enigma Variations*, Cello Concerto, *Pomp and Circumstance* marches

bio:
Elgar was born in 1857 in Lower Broadheath, a village near Worcester, the son of a piano tuner who kept a music shop in the city. Apart from piano and violin lessons, he was almost entirely self-taught. For years he earned his living locally: teaching, playing the violin in festival orchestras, conducting, and writing music for whatever ensembles were at hand, from a wind quintet to the band of a nearby asylum. In 1889 he married Caroline Alice Roberts, a general’s daughter eight years older than him, whose family disapproved of the match. She became his business manager and a perceptive critic of his music.

Success came late. In 1899, at 42, the *Enigma Variations*, a set of musical portraits of his friends, made his name, and *The Dream of Gerontius* followed in 1900. He was knighted in 1904. His First Symphony (1908) was played around a hundred times in little more than a year, and the Violin Concerto followed in 1910. During the First World War “Land of Hope and Glory”, sung to a tune from his first *Pomp and Circumstance* march, grew more popular than ever, though Elgar wished in vain for less nationalistic words.

After the war his music went out of fashion. In a cottage in the Sussex woods he wrote three chamber works and then the Cello Concerto (1919), his last major work. Alice died in 1920 and he completed no more large-scale pieces, though he became one of the first composers to take the gramophone seriously, recording much of his own music, and in 1924 was made Master of the King’s Music. He died in Worcester in 1934, leaving sketches for a Third Symphony that the composer Anthony Payne later completed.
birthdayNote: In 1932, aged 75, Elgar recorded the Violin Concerto with the 16-year-old Yehudi Menuhin. The old composer and the young violinist became friends.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1857, in Lower Broadheath.

name: Ulvi Cemal Erkin
bio:
Erkin was born in Istanbul in 1906, in the last years of the Ottoman Empire. His mother played the piano and his elder brother the violin; he lost his father at the age of seven, and the family went to live with his grandfather. He had piano lessons from childhood and studied at the Galatasaray Lycée. In 1925, at 19, he won a scholarship from the young Republic to study in Paris. There he studied the piano with Isidor Philipp and Camille Decreus at the Conservatoire, harmony and counterpoint with Jean and Noël Gallon, and composition with Nadia Boulanger at the École Normale de Musique.

In 1930 he returned to teach the piano and harmony at the Musiki Muallim Mektebi in Ankara, a school for music teachers that became the Ankara State Conservatory in 1936. He taught there for the rest of his life, more than forty years, was its director from 1949 to 1951 and trained generations of Turkish pianists. In 1932 he married the pianist Ferhunde Remzi, who became the leading interpreter of his piano music. In November 1936 he travelled with Béla Bartók, Ahmed Adnan Saygun and Necil Kazım Akses to collect folk songs around Adana and Osmaniye. With Saygun, Akses, Cemal Reşit Rey and Hasan Ferit Alnar he is counted among the “Turkish Five”, composers born within a few years of one another who joined European forms with the modes of Turkish music and the uneven rhythms of Anatolian folk dance.

His dance rhapsody *Köçekçe* (1943), inspired by the köçek dancers of Ottoman entertainments and built from dance tunes from across Anatolia, is still his most performed work. His Piano Concerto, with Ferhunde Erkin as soloist, shared a national composition prize in 1943, and his Violin Concerto (1946–47) was first heard at the opening of Ankara’s opera house in 1948; he also wrote two symphonies and chamber and piano music, and conducted his works at home and abroad. His early music shows the influence of Debussy and Ravel; later he found a voice of his own, with clear forms, chords built on fourths and fifths, and melodies and rhythms drawn from Anatolia. In 1971 he was named a State Artist. He died of a heart attack in Ankara on 15 September 1972, still teaching, and is buried in the city’s Karşıyaka Cemetery.
birthdayNote: When Erkin won a place at the Paris Conservatoire, the musicologist Mahmut Ragıp Gazimihal hailed it as a first: a young Turk had got in through the entrance competition.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1906, in Istanbul.

name: Manuel de Falla

facts.label: bestKnownFor
facts.value: *Nights in the Gardens of Spain*, *El amor brujo*, *The Three-Cornered Hat*

bio:
Falla was born in Cádiz, in the far south of Spain, in 1876. At the Madrid Conservatory he studied the piano with José Tragó and composition with Felipe Pedrell, who encouraged his interest in the music of Andalusia, above all flamenco and *cante jondo*, its “deep song”. His one-act opera *La vida breve* won a national competition in 1905, but the promised production at the Teatro Real in Madrid never came.

In 1907 he moved to Paris, where he stayed for seven years. There he came to know Debussy, Ravel, Paul Dukas, Stravinsky and the Spanish composer Isaac Albéniz, and *La vida breve* was finally staged, in Nice, in 1913. When the First World War broke out he returned to Madrid, and the next years brought his best-known works: the ballet with songs *El amor brujo* (1915), *Nights in the Gardens of Spain* (1916) and *The Three-Cornered Hat*, staged by Sergei Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes with sets and costumes by Pablo Picasso.

From 1921 he lived in Granada, below the Alhambra. In 1922, with the young poet Federico García Lorca, he organised a festival of *cante jondo* there to save the old songs, and his music grew leaner and more classical: the puppet opera *El retablo de maese Pedro* (1923) and a Harpsichord Concerto (1926). He spent his last twenty years on *Atlántida*, a vast cantata he never finished. After the Spanish Civil War he left for Argentina in 1939 and refused offers to come back. He died in Alta Gracia on 14 November 1946, nine days before his 70th birthday, and was buried in the crypt of Cádiz Cathedral.
birthdayNote: In 1922 Falla organised a contest of *cante jondo*, the “deep song” of Andalusian flamenco, in the grounds of the Alhambra, hoping to save an art he feared was dying.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1876, in Cádiz.

name: Gabriel Fauré
bio:
Fauré was born in 1845 in Pamiers, in the foothills of the Pyrenees, the youngest of six children of a schoolmaster. He was the only one of them with a gift for music, and he found it on the harmonium of the chapel at his father’s teacher-training college. At nine he was sent to Paris, to the École Niedermeyer, a boarding school that trained church organists and choirmasters. There, from 1861, his piano teacher was Camille Saint-Saëns, who showed his pupils the music of Schumann, Liszt and Wagner and became Fauré’s friend for life. Fauré left in 1865 with a prize for his *Cantique de Jean Racine*.

For decades he earned his living at the organ and by teaching. His first post, in Rennes, ended when he arrived to play at Mass one Sunday still in evening clothes after a ball. After serving in the Franco-Prussian War he helped to found the Société nationale de musique in 1871, and in 1877 he became choirmaster of the Madeleine in Paris, where he later became chief organist. His publisher bought his songs outright for small sums, and composition had to wait for the summer holidays. Yet these years produced the songs that made him a master of the French mélodie, among them *Après un rêve* and *Clair de lune*, the *Pavane* and the [[requiem|Requiem]]. In 1896 he became professor of composition at the Paris Conservatoire, where his pupils included Ravel and Nadia Boulanger.

In 1905 he was made director of the Conservatoire, and he modernised it so firmly that the old guard called him “Robespierre”. From around this time he was slowly going deaf, and high and low notes reached him painfully out of tune. He still wrote some of his finest music, the opera *Pénélope* (1913), late songs, piano pieces and chamber music, much of it composed in hotels by the Swiss lakes. He retired in 1920, was honoured with a national tribute in 1922, and finished his only string quartet in September 1924. He died in Paris on 4 November 1924, aged 79, and was given a state funeral at the Madeleine. Aaron Copland called him “the Brahms of France”.
birthdayNote: As a small boy in the south of France, Fauré slipped away to play the harmonium in a school chapel whenever he could. An old blind woman who came to listen told his father that the boy had a gift.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1845, in Pamiers.

name: César Franck

facts.label: bestKnownFor
facts.value: Violin Sonata, Symphony in D minor, organ music

bio:
Franck was born in Liège, in today’s Belgium, in 1822. His father, a bank clerk, wanted him to become a touring piano prodigy like Liszt, arranged his first concerts at the age of eleven and in 1835 took him to Paris to study. The virtuoso career never came. Franck broke with his father to marry one of his piano pupils, Félicité Saillot, in February 1848, in the middle of a revolution: the wedding party had to climb over the barricades to reach the church.

For the rest of his life he earned his living as a church organist and teacher. From 1859 he was organist of the church of Sainte-Clotilde in Paris, famous for his improvisations, and from 1872 professor of organ at the Paris Conservatoire, for which he took French nationality. A devoted circle of pupils, among them Vincent d’Indy, Ernest Chausson and Henri Duparc, gathered around the man they called “Père Franck”.

Almost all the music he is remembered for came in his last dozen years: the Piano Quintet, the Violin Sonata, the Symphony in D minor and the organ *Chorals*, finished a few weeks before his death. Many of these works use [[cyclic-form|cyclic form]], with themes that return from one movement to the next. Success came late: his String Quartet, first played in April 1890, was his first unqualified public triumph. He died in Paris that November.
birthdayNote: The Violin Sonata was a wedding present for Eugène Ysaÿe. At its public premiere, in a Brussels gallery where no lamps were allowed, the last movements were played from memory in the fading light.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1822, in Liège.

name: George Gershwin

facts.label: bestKnownFor
facts.value: *Rhapsody in Blue*, *An American in Paris*, the opera *Porgy and Bess*

bio:
Gershwin was born Jacob Gershwine in Brooklyn in 1898, the second son of Jewish immigrants from the Russian Empire, and grew up in the crowded streets of New York. Music meant nothing to him until he was about ten. Then his parents bought a piano for his older brother Ira, and it was George who could not leave it alone. His teacher Charles Hambitzer taught him a proper technique and took him to orchestral concerts. At fifteen he left school to work as a “song plugger” in Tin Pan Alley, playing a publisher’s new songs for customers all day for fifteen dollars a week, and he began to cut piano rolls and write songs of his own. In 1919 Al Jolson sang his “Swanee”, and it became a national hit.

In 1924 the bandleader Paul Whiteman persuaded him to write a concert piece for a jazz band, and *Rhapsody in Blue* made him famous overnight. In the same years he and Ira, who wrote the lyrics, filled Broadway with musicals, among them *Lady, Be Good!*, *Funny Face* and *Girl Crazy*, and songs such as “Fascinating Rhythm”, “Embraceable You” and “I Got Rhythm”; their *Of Thee I Sing* was the first musical to win the Pulitzer Prize for Drama. He also kept writing for the concert hall: a Piano Concerto in F (1925) and, after a stay in Paris, *An American in Paris* (1928). There he asked Nadia Boulanger and Ravel for lessons; both declined, fearing that strict training would spoil his style.

His most ambitious work, the opera *Porgy and Bess* (1935), written with Ira and the novelist DuBose Heyward and set among the Black community of Charleston, was a commercial failure at first; it has since become one of the best-known American operas, and its song “Summertime” a standard. In 1936 he moved to Hollywood to write film music, including *Shall We Dance* for Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers, and played tennis with Arnold Schoenberg. Early in 1937 he began to suffer headaches and blackouts. On 9 July he collapsed; a brain tumour was found too late, and he died in Los Angeles on 11 July 1937, aged 38.
birthdayNote: The clarinet glissando that opens *Rhapsody in Blue* began, the story goes, as a joke in rehearsal by the clarinettist Ross Gorman. Gershwin liked it and kept it.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1898, in Brooklyn.

name: Edvard Grieg
bio:
Grieg was born in Bergen, on Norway’s west coast, in 1843. His mother, Gesine, was a music teacher and gave him his first piano lessons when he was six. In 1858 the famous Norwegian violinist Ole Bull, a friend of the family, persuaded his parents to send the fifteen-year-old to the Leipzig Conservatory. In 1860 he survived pleurisy and tuberculosis, which left him with a ruined left lung for the rest of his life.

From 1863 he spent three years in Copenhagen, where he became close friends with the young Norwegian composer Rikard Nordraak; when Nordraak died in 1866, Grieg wrote a funeral march for him. In 1867 he married his cousin, the soprano Nina Hagerup, who sang his songs for the rest of his life. The Piano Concerto, written the next year, made his name across Europe, and his music for Henrik Ibsen’s play *Peer Gynt*, with “Morning Mood” and “In the Hall of the Mountain King”, made it known everywhere.

Grieg did his best work in small forms: songs, and sixty-six *Lyric Pieces* for piano, published in ten books. Norwegian folk dances and fiddle tunes run through his music. He suppressed his only symphony and completed only one concerto. He died in Bergen in 1907. His house, Troldhaugen, is now a museum, and his and Nina’s ashes rest in a crypt in the rock nearby.
birthdayNote: Grieg could not bear to hear “In the Hall of the Mountain King”, a piece that, in the composer’s words, “reeks of cowpats”. Listeners have never agreed: it closes the *Peer Gynt* Suite No. 1.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1843, in Bergen.

name: George Frideric Handel

facts.label: symphonies
facts.value: None (the form came after his time)

bio:
Handel was born in Halle, in Saxony, in 1685, the same year as Bach. His father, a barber-surgeon who served the local court, wanted him to study law, and in 1702 he enrolled at the University of Halle, but music won. He went to Hamburg, played in the orchestra of its opera house and saw his first operas staged there in 1705. He then spent several years in Italy, writing operas and church music, before becoming music director to the Elector of Hanover in 1710.

Within months he was in London, where his Italian opera *Rinaldo* was a great success in 1711, and in 1712 he settled there for good. When the Elector became King George I of Great Britain in 1714, Handel was already at home in London. His *Water Music* was played for the king on the Thames in 1717. For years he wrote and produced Italian operas for the London nobility, and in 1727 he became a British subject; in the same year he wrote *Zadok the Priest* for the coronation of George II, an anthem sung at every British coronation since.

When Italian opera lost its public in the late 1730s, he turned to oratorios, dramatic works in English for soloists and chorus. *Messiah*, first performed in Dublin in 1742, became the most famous, and he gave it for years in aid of the Foundling Hospital, a London home for abandoned children. From 1752 he was blind. He died at his house in Brook Street in April 1759, a rich and respected man, and was given a state funeral in Westminster Abbey.
birthdayNote: The public rehearsal of the *Music for the Royal Fireworks* in 1749 drew a crowd said to number twelve thousand and jammed London Bridge for hours. On the night itself, a pavilion caught fire.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1685 (Old Style), in Halle.

name: Joseph Haydn
bio:
Haydn was born in 1732 in Rohrau, a village in Lower Austria near the Hungarian border, the son of a wheelwright. At about eight he was sent to Vienna to sing in the choir of St Stephen’s Cathedral. When his voice broke he was dismissed, and for years he scraped a living by teaching and playing while he taught himself to compose. For a time he worked as accompanist and valet to the Italian composer Nicola Porpora, from whom, he said, he learned the true fundamentals of composition.

In 1761 he joined the household of the Esterházy princes, and from 1766 he directed their music for almost thirty years, much of the time at the remote palace of Eszterháza in Hungary. He had an orchestra, singers and an opera house at his disposal and could experiment as he liked. Cut off from the world, he later said, he was “forced to become original”. There he wrote most of his symphonies and string quartets and made both into central forms of the Classical style. He became a close friend of Mozart, and in 1792 the young Beethoven came to Vienna to study with him.

After Prince Nikolaus died in 1790, Haydn travelled to London with the concert manager Johann Peter Salomon, in 1791–92 and again in 1794–95. His twelve London symphonies were a triumph, and Oxford made him an honorary doctor. Back in Vienna he wrote the oratorios *The Creation* and *The Seasons*, and the hymn for the emperor whose tune is now the German national anthem. He died in Vienna in May 1809, while the city was occupied by Napoleon’s army. He is often called the father of the symphony and of the string quartet: he did not invent them, but he showed what they could do.
birthdayNote: In the *Farewell* Symphony the players stop one by one and leave, until two violins remain: Haydn’s hint to the prince that the musicians wanted to go home. The story goes that the court left the next day.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1732, in Rohrau.

name: Gustav Holst

facts.label: symphonies
facts.value: Two: the *Cotswolds* Symphony and the *Choral Symphony*

facts.label: bestKnownFor
facts.value: *The Planets*, *St Paul’s Suite*, the carol tune for *In the Bleak Midwinter*

bio:
Holst was born Gustavus Theodore von Holst in Cheltenham in 1874. His father’s family, of Swedish, Latvian and German descent, had produced a professional musician in each of the three previous generations; his father, Adolph, was an organist, choirmaster and teacher. Holst hoped to become a pianist, but neuritis in his right arm stopped him, and he turned to composition. At the Royal College of Music he studied with Charles Villiers Stanford, and in 1895 he met Ralph Vaughan Williams, who became his lifelong friend and closest critic. To earn a living he played the trombone, as first trombone of the Carl Rosa Opera Company from 1898 and with the Scottish Orchestra.

Teaching filled most of his life. From 1905 until his death he was director of music at St Paul’s Girls’ School in London, where a soundproof music room gave him a place to compose, and from 1907 to 1924 he led the music at Morley College, an evening college for working adults. He learned Sanskrit to make his own translations of Hindu texts for the chamber opera *Savitri* and the *Rig Veda* hymns, and the writer Clifford Bax introduced him to astrology, the starting point of *The Planets* (1914–16). In 1918 he dropped the “von” from his name and went to Salonica as a music organiser for the YMCA, working with soldiers waiting to go home.

After the war *The Planets* made him internationally famous, a fame he found unwelcome and struggled against for the rest of his life. His later music grew sparer and more austere: *The Hymn of Jesus* (1917), the *Choral Symphony* and *Egdon Heath* (1927), a bleak picture of Thomas Hardy’s moorland. His daughter Imogen, born in 1907, became a musician and his biographer. He died in London on 25 May 1934, aged 59, after an operation, and his ashes lie in Chichester Cathedral.
birthdayNote: Holst called astrology his “pet vice” and cast his friends’ horoscopes. *The Planets* grew out of that hobby: each movement is a planet’s character in astrology, not in astronomy.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1874, in Cheltenham.

name: Franz Liszt

facts.label: symphonies
facts.value: Two: *A Faust Symphony* and the *Dante Symphony*

facts.label: bestKnownFor
facts.value: Piano Sonata in B minor, *Hungarian Rhapsodies*, symphonic poems

bio:
Liszt was born in 1811 in Raiding (Doborján in Hungarian), a village in the Kingdom of Hungary, where his father worked as a steward for Prince Esterházy. He was a child prodigy. In Vienna he studied piano with Carl Czerny and composition with Antonio Salieri, and in 1823 the family settled in Paris. In 1832 he heard the violinist Niccolò Paganini, and set out to do for the piano what Paganini had done for the violin.

He became the most celebrated pianist in Europe. He toured all over the continent, gave the solo piano recital its modern form, and caused such excitement that the poet Heinrich Heine coined the word “Lisztomania”. His daughter Cosima, from his relationship with the Countess Marie d’Agoult, later married Richard Wagner. In 1848 he settled in Weimar as court music director, with Princess Carolyne zu Sayn-Wittgenstein. There he conducted new music by Wagner and Berlioz, including the premiere of *Lohengrin* in 1850, and wrote his own most ambitious works: the symphonic poems, the *Faust Symphony* and the Piano Sonata in B minor.

In the 1860s he moved to Rome and in 1865 took minor orders in the Catholic Church, becoming “Abbé Liszt”. From 1872 he divided his year between Rome, Weimar and Budapest, where he helped to found the music academy that now bears his name. He taught hundreds of pianists and never charged for lessons. His late piano pieces are sparse and strange, and look ahead to the music of the 20th century. He died in Bayreuth in 1886.
birthdayNote: At the height of “Lisztomania”, fans fought over Liszt’s gloves and handkerchiefs, and one admirer had a discarded cigar stump set in a locket. The pop concert is older than it looks.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1811, in Raiding.

name: Gustav Mahler
bio:
Mahler was born in 1860 in Kaliště, a village in Bohemia, into a German-speaking Jewish family, and grew up in the nearby town of Jihlava. Many of his parents’ fourteen children died young, and death and loss echo all through his music. As a boy he loved folk songs and the military bands of the local barracks, sounds that later found their way into his symphonies. At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition.

He became one of the greatest conductors of his time. In 1897 he took charge of the Vienna Court Opera, having converted from Judaism to Catholicism shortly before, as the post effectively required. He was a fierce perfectionist, and his demand for fresh, meticulously rehearsed performances won him admirers and enemies in equal measure. For ten demanding years he transformed the company, and he composed in the summers, in small composing huts by lakes and in the mountains.

Mahler is said to have told Sibelius that a symphony must be like the world: it must embrace everything. His symphonies are vast, mixing folk songs, marches, birdsong and moments of deep stillness. After leaving Vienna he conducted in New York, at the Metropolitan Opera and the New York Philharmonic. He died in Vienna in 1911, aged 50, leaving his Tenth Symphony unfinished.
birthdayNote: The Fourth Symphony ends with a soprano singing a child’s picture of heaven: a great feast, with angels baking the bread. A gentle way into Mahler’s music on the composer’s birthday.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1860, in Kaliště.

name: Felix Mendelssohn

facts.label: symphonies
facts.value: Five numbered, plus 13 early string symphonies

facts.label: bestKnownFor
facts.value: Violin Concerto, *A Midsummer Night's Dream*, *Songs without Words*

bio:
Mendelssohn was born in Hamburg in 1809 into a wealthy, cultured family; his grandfather was the Jewish philosopher Moses Mendelssohn. The family moved to Berlin when he was two, the children were baptised as Protestants, and his parents later added the surname Bartholdy. Felix and his older sister Fanny, herself a gifted composer, grew up surrounded by music. At 16 he wrote his String Octet, and at 17 the overture to *A Midsummer Night’s Dream*.

In 1829, aged 20, he conducted Bach’s *St Matthew Passion* in Berlin, a performance that helped bring Bach’s music back into concert life. He travelled widely, to Italy and many times to Britain, and the journeys gave him the *Italian* Symphony, the *Scottish* Symphony and the *Hebrides* overture, inspired by Fingal’s Cave. In 1835 he became director of the Gewandhaus Orchestra in Leipzig, and in 1843 he founded the Leipzig Conservatory.

He worked at a furious pace as composer, conductor, pianist and organiser. His oratorio *Elijah* was first performed in Birmingham in 1846. In May 1847 his sister Fanny died suddenly, and less than six months later, on 4 November, he died in Leipzig after a series of strokes, aged 38. Later in the century his polished, light-filled music fell out of fashion, partly through antisemitism, but works such as the Violin Concerto never left the concert hall.
birthdayNote: Travelling in the Scottish islands in 1829, Mendelssohn sent home a letter with a few bars of music in it: the opening of what became *The Hebrides*. You hear them in its first seconds.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1809, in Hamburg.

name: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
bio:
Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, the son of Leopold, a violinist and composer who was also a gifted teacher. Wolfgang was writing little pieces by the age of five, and as a child he toured the courts and concert halls of Europe with his father and his older sister, Nannerl, a brilliant keyboard player herself. Those years on the road filled his ears with every musical style of the day, from Italian opera to German counterpoint.

In 1781 he broke with his employer, the Archbishop of Salzburg, and settled in Vienna as a freelance musician, a rare and risky move at the time. He earned his living by teaching, playing his own piano concertos at subscription concerts and selling his music. The Vienna years brought *The Marriage of Figaro*, *Don Giovanni* and *The Magic Flute*, and his last three symphonies, all written within a few weeks in the summer of 1788.

He died in Vienna in December 1791, aged 35, with his *Requiem* unfinished; his pupil Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed it. What lasts is the feeling that nothing in his music is forced. Melodies that sound effortless turn out to be carefully built, and even the brightest pages can cloud over in a bar or two. That is why his music works on a first hearing and still rewards the hundredth.
birthdayNote: In 1784 Mozart bought a pet starling that could whistle a tune from a new piano concerto, and wrote it into the household accounts. When the bird died three years later, Mozart buried it in the garden, with a poem.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1756, in Salzburg.

name: Modest Mussorgsky

facts.label: bestKnownFor
facts.value: *Boris Godunov*, *Pictures at an Exhibition*, *Night on Bald Mountain*

bio:
Mussorgsky was born in 1839 at Karevo, a country estate in the Pskov region of western Russia, into a wealthy family of landowning nobles. His mother gave him his first piano lessons when he was six. At ten he was sent to school in St Petersburg, and at thirteen he entered the Cadet School of the Guards, the usual path for a boy of his class. In 1856 he became an officer in the Preobrazhensky Regiment. That winter he met the composer Alexander Dargomyzhsky, and soon afterwards Mily Balakirev, who taught him musical form. In 1858 he resigned his commission to devote himself to music.

The emancipation of the serfs in 1861 cost his family half its estate, and for most of his life Mussorgsky earned his living as a low-ranking civil servant, composing in the time left over. He belonged to the circle around Balakirev later known as The Five, who wanted a music that sounded Russian. He wanted his vocal music to follow the natural rhythms of Russian speech, and his opera *Boris Godunov* did exactly that. The Mariinsky Theatre rejected its first version in 1871; a revised version reached the stage in February 1874. In the same year he wrote *Pictures at an Exhibition* for piano, in memory of his friend Viktor Hartmann, an architect and painter.

Heavy drinking, which had begun to trouble him in the 1860s, damaged his health and his work. He left the operas *Khovanshchina* and *The Fair at Sorochyntsi* unfinished. In March 1881, days before his death, Ilya Repin painted his portrait in a St Petersburg military hospital. He died a week after his 42nd birthday. His friend Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov completed and edited much of his music, smoothing its rough harmonies, and it was mostly in those versions that the world first came to know him. Ravel’s orchestration of *Pictures at an Exhibition* (1922) made the suite famous in the concert hall.
birthdayNote: Mussorgsky finished the first *Night on Bald Mountain* on St John’s Eve 1867, the very night of the witches’ sabbath it depicts. The version we usually hear is Rimsky-Korsakov’s, made after Mussorgsky died.

name: Johann Pachelbel

facts.label: symphonies
facts.value: None (the form came after his time)

facts.label: bestKnownFor
facts.value: *Canon in D*, organ chorales and fugues, *Hexachordum Apollinis*

bio:
Pachelbel was born in Nuremberg in 1653, the son of a wine merchant. After brief studies at the University of Altdorf and at a grammar school in Regensburg, he was working by 1673 as deputy organist of St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. He spent five years there, and although he was a Lutheran, the Italian and south German music of the Catholic south shaped his style for good.

In 1677 he became court organist at Eisenach, where he grew close to the Bach family, and in 1678 he moved to Erfurt as organist of the Predigerkirche. In twelve years there he became one of the leading organ composers in Germany. He taught Johann Christoph Bach, Johann Sebastian’s eldest brother, and was godfather to one of the Bach daughters. His first wife and their son died of plague in 1683. After short posts in Stuttgart and Gotha, Nuremberg invited him home in 1695 as organist of St Sebaldus, without the usual audition.

He died in Nuremberg in March 1706, aged 52. In his lifetime he was famous above all for his organ music, more than two hundred pieces, many of them chorale preludes and fugues, and for *Hexachordum Apollinis* (1699), a set of keyboard variations dedicated to Buxtehude. He also wrote about a hundred vocal works; only a little of his chamber music survives. Today he is known mainly for his [[canon|canon]] in D, a piece that was rediscovered only in the 20th century.

name: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina

facts.label: symphonies
facts.value: None (the form did not exist yet)

facts.label: bestKnownFor
facts.value: *Missa Papae Marcelli*, more than 100 masses, motets

bio:
Palestrina took his name from his birthplace, a small town in the hills east of Rome, where he was born around 1525. As a boy he sang in the choir of the basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore in Rome, and from 1544 he was organist of the cathedral of his home town. When its bishop became Pope Julius III, he brought Palestrina to Rome in 1551 as choirmaster of the Cappella Giulia at St Peter’s. His first book of masses, dedicated to the pope in 1554, was the first such book by a composer born in Italy; until then the leading church composers in Italy came from the Low Countries, France or Spain.

In 1555 a new pope ruled that the papal singers must be clergy, and Palestrina, who was married with children, had to leave the papal choir. He went on to lead the music at St John Lateran and then at Santa Maria Maggiore, and in 1571 he returned to St Peter’s, where he stayed for the rest of his life. The 1570s brought heavy losses: outbreaks of plague killed his brother, two of his sons and his wife. He then married a wealthy widow, which gave him the security to compose and publish freely.

He died in Rome in February 1594 and was buried in St Peter’s, in a coffin whose lead plate called him “Prince of Music”. He left more than a hundred masses and some three hundred [[motet|motet]]s. His calm, carefully controlled way of weaving voices together became the model for teaching [[counterpoint|counterpoint]] for centuries, above all through Johann Joseph Fux’s textbook of 1725, and Bach copied and performed his masses. A legend that he saved church music at the Council of Trent kept his name famous, although historians have found no evidence for it.

name: Sergei Prokofiev

facts.label: bestKnownFor
facts.value: *Peter and the Wolf*, *Romeo and Juliet*, the *Classical* Symphony

bio:
Prokofiev was born in 1891 on a country estate at Sontsovka, in what is now eastern Ukraine, where his father managed the land. His mother was a keen pianist, and he wrote his first piano piece at five and his first opera at nine. At thirteen he entered the St Petersburg Conservatory, where he was younger than most of his classmates and soon known as a rebel. His spiky, percussive piano music and his first two piano concertos caused scandals; he finished his studies in 1914 by winning the Conservatory’s piano prize with his own First Concerto.

In 1917, the year of the revolutions, he wrote his *Classical* Symphony and his First Violin Concerto. In 1918, with official permission, he left Russia and spent the next years abroad, first in the United States, where his opera *The Love for Three Oranges* was staged in Chicago in 1921, then in Paris, working for Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes and touring as a pianist. In 1923 he married the Spanish singer Lina Codina; they had two sons.

In 1936 he settled with his family in Moscow. That year he wrote *Peter and the Wolf*; his Soviet successes also included the ballet *Romeo and Juliet* and his music for Eisenstein’s film *Alexander Nevsky* (1938). During the war he worked on the opera *War and Peace*. In 1948 the Soviet authorities condemned his music as “formalist”, and the same year his former wife Lina was arrested and charged with espionage. He died in Moscow on 5 March 1953, on the same day as Stalin; the crowds mourning the dictator made it hard even to carry his coffin through the streets.
birthdayNote: Prokofiev celebrated on 23 April all life long. The birth certificate, found only after the composer’s death, says 27 April: four days later, and the day we keep.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1891, in Sontsovka.

name: Sergei Rachmaninoff

facts.label: bestKnownFor
facts.value: Piano Concertos Nos. 2 and 3, *Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini*

bio:
Rachmaninoff was born in 1873 into a landowning family in the Novgorod region of north-west Russia. His father’s debts cost the family its estates, and in 1882 they moved to a small flat in St Petersburg. After two unsettled years at the conservatory there, at twelve he was sent to Moscow to live with Nikolai Zverev, a strict piano teacher who took in a few pupils as boarders. He graduated from the Moscow Conservatory in 1892 with the Great Gold Medal. His student opera *Aleko* won Tchaikovsky’s praise, and his Prelude in C-sharp minor soon made his name far beyond Russia.

In 1897 the premiere of his First Symphony was a disaster, and for three years he wrote almost nothing. Treatment with the physician Nikolai Dahl helped him back to work, and the Second Piano Concerto (1901), dedicated to Dahl, became his most popular piece. The years that followed were full: in 1902 he married his cousin Natalia Satina, he conducted at the Bolshoi Theatre, he spent three winters in Dresden, where he wrote his Second Symphony, and in 1909 he toured America with his Third Piano Concerto, written for that tour.

The Russian Revolution ended that life. In December 1917 he left Russia with his family and never returned. To support them he became a touring pianist, one of the greatest of his time, and settled in the United States. He composed much less, partly in a villa he built on Lake Lucerne, where he wrote the *Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini* (1934). His last work was the *Symphonic Dances* (1940). He died in Beverly Hills on 28 March 1943, four days before his seventieth birthday.
birthdayNote: Stravinsky is said to have called Rachmaninoff “a six-and-a-half-foot scowl”. The music tells a warmer story: try the slow movement of the Second Piano Concerto.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1873, in the Novgorod Governorate.

name: Maurice Ravel
bio:
Ravel was born in 1875 in Ciboure, a Basque town in south-west France about eleven miles from the Spanish border. His mother was Basque; his father was an engineer and inventor from near the Swiss border. The family moved to Paris when Maurice was three months old, and he grew up there, studying at the Paris Conservatoire. The conservative establishment never warmed to him: he tried five times for the Prix de Rome, and his elimination in 1905, by then an established composer, caused a public scandal.

He worked slowly and with great care, and many of his pieces exist twice, first for piano and later for orchestra. He became one of the great masters of orchestration: *Daphnis et Chloé* (1912), written for Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes, and his orchestral version of Mussorgsky’s *Pictures at an Exhibition* (1922) are showpieces for any orchestra. When war came in 1914 he insisted on serving, and in 1915, aged forty, he became an army lorry driver, carrying munitions at night under bombardment. His piano suite *Le Tombeau de Couperin* honours friends killed in the war, one in each movement.

By the 1920s he was regarded as France’s greatest living composer. In 1928 he toured North America for four months, and that same year wrote *Boléro*, which made him more famous than ever, to his own surprise. He wrote no symphonies, but two piano concertos, two operas, ballets, chamber music and songs. From the early 1930s a neurological illness slowly took away his ability to write. He died in Paris on 28 December 1937, after brain surgery, aged 62.
birthdayNote: Ravel called *Boléro* an experiment in “orchestral tissue without music”: one tune, one rhythm, one long crescendo. It became Ravel’s most famous work, to the composer’s own surprise.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1875, in Ciboure.

name: Ottorino Respighi

facts.label: bestKnownFor
facts.value: *Fountains of Rome*, *Pines of Rome*, *Roman Festivals*, *Ancient Airs and Dances*

bio:
Respighi was born in Bologna in 1879. His father, a post-office worker, was a fine pianist who taught music, and gave the boy his first lessons on the piano and the violin. At twelve he entered the Liceo Musicale of Bologna, where he studied violin, viola and composition; he took his violin diploma in 1899. The following winter he went to St Petersburg as principal viola of the Imperial opera orchestra, and there he took lessons in orchestration from Rimsky-Korsakov, whose brilliant use of the orchestra shaped his own. When he finished his composition studies in 1901, his teacher Giuseppe Martucci said: “Respighi is not a pupil, Respighi is a master.” He was a voracious reader and came to read literature in eleven languages.

For the next decade he earned his living mainly as a violinist and viola player in Bologna, while composing songs and operas and arranging forgotten Italian music of the 17th and 18th centuries, a lifelong passion. In 1913 he moved to Rome as professor of composition at the Liceo Musicale di Santa Cecilia. One of his pupils was the singer Elsa Olivieri-Sangiacomo; they married in 1919, and she became his closest companion and, after his death, the keeper of his music. *Fountains of Rome* was coolly received at its premiere in 1917, but in 1918 Toscanini conducted it in Milan and it made Respighi famous. His suites *Ancient Airs and Dances*, freely arranged from old lute pieces, and the ballet *La Boutique fantasque*, made from piano pieces by Rossini for Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes, followed.

In 1923 he became the first director of the Conservatorio di Santa Cecilia, but he disliked the paperwork and resigned in 1926, while still teaching composition until 1935. *Pines of Rome* (1924) and *Roman Festivals* (1928) completed his Roman trilogy, and from 1925 he toured the United States and South America as conductor and pianist in his own music. He kept a cautious distance from Mussolini’s regime, which nevertheless honoured him and used his music. At the end of 1935, while writing the opera *Lucrezia*, he fell ill with an infection of the heart that could not then be cured, and he died in Rome on 18 April 1936, aged 56. Elsa outlived him by almost sixty years.
birthdayNote: In *Pines of Rome* Respighi asks for a gramophone record of a real nightingale, singing in the moonlit pines: one of the first uses of recorded sound in a concert work.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1879, in Bologna.

name: Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov
bio:
Rimsky-Korsakov was born in 1844 in Tikhvin, east of St Petersburg, into a noble family. As a boy he loved the sea long before he had seen it, from books and from his older brother’s stories of the navy, and he trained as a naval officer himself. At eighteen he sailed on the clipper *Almaz* on a voyage that lasted two years and eight months, and he wrote the slow movement of his First Symphony during a stop in England. Back on shore he joined the circle of composers around Mily Balakirev, later known as The Five, who wanted a music that sounded Russian rather than German.

In 1871, aged 27 and still a naval officer, he became professor of composition and orchestration at the St Petersburg Conservatory. He admitted that he knew little theory and had to teach himself as he went, becoming, as he put it, the conservatory’s best pupil. He taught there for 35 years. His pupils included Glazunov, Prokofiev and Respighi, and he taught Stravinsky privately. He also prepared his friends’ unfinished or unpolished works for performance, among them Mussorgsky’s operas and Borodin’s *Prince Igor*.

His own music is famous for its brilliant orchestral colour: *Capriccio espagnol*, the *Russian Easter Festival Overture* and *Scheherazade*, the last two written in the summer of 1888, and fifteen operas drawn from Russian fairy tales and legends. In 1905 he defended students who were protesting during the revolution, was dismissed from the conservatory, and for a time the police banned his music, which caused an outcry in Russia and abroad. He died in 1908 at his country estate near Luga, south of St Petersburg.
birthdayNote: In *Scheherazade* the solo violin is the storyteller, returning between the tales. Rimsky-Korsakov later dropped the movement titles, so that listeners could imagine the stories for themselves.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1844, in Tikhvin.

name: Joaquín Rodrigo
bio:
Rodrigo was born in 1901 in Sagunto, near Valencia. At the age of three he caught diphtheria and lost his sight almost completely. He began to study music at eight, the piano and the violin first, then harmony and composition in Valencia; all his life he wrote his music in Braille, and it was copied out for publication. In 1927 he went to Paris to study composition with Paul Dukas at the École Normale de Musique. There he met the pianist Victoria Kamhi, born in Istanbul, and they married in 1933. She gave up her own career to work at his side for the rest of her life.

During the Spanish Civil War the couple lived abroad, in France and Germany. In Paris, early in 1939, Rodrigo wrote the *Concierto de Aranjuez* for the guitarist Regino Sainz de la Maza, although he was a pianist and never played the guitar himself. He returned to Spain that year, and the concerto’s premiere in Barcelona in November 1940 made him famous almost overnight. From 1947 he taught the history of music at the University of Madrid, in a chair named after Manuel de Falla; among his students was the Turkish composer and pianist Yüksel Koptagel.

The success of the concerto brought requests from famous soloists: *Fantasía para un gentilhombre* (1954) for Andrés Segovia, and concertos for the harpist Nicanor Zabaleta, the flautist James Galway, the cellist Julian Lloyd Webber and the guitar family of the Romeros. His music, melodious and full of the dances and colours of old Spain, stayed close to tradition, and the fame of the *Concierto de Aranjuez* overshadowed almost everything else he wrote. In 1991 King Juan Carlos I made him Marquess of the Gardens of Aranjuez. Victoria died in 1997; Rodrigo died at home in Madrid on 6 July 1999, aged 97, and they are buried together in Aranjuez.
birthdayNote: Rodrigo was born on St Cecilia’s Day, the feast of the patron saint of music. A fitting start for a composer who never played the guitar, yet wrote the *Concierto de Aranjuez*.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1901, in Sagunto.

name: Gioachino Rossini
bio:
Rossini was born in Pesaro, on the Adriatic coast of Italy, in 1792, the son of two musicians: his father played the trumpet and the horn, his mother was a singer. He grew up partly in Lugo, where a priest’s library introduced him to the music of Haydn and Mozart, then little known in Italy, and he went on to study at the music school in Bologna. His first opera was staged in Venice in 1810, when he was eighteen.

Between 1810 and 1823 he wrote 34 operas for Italian theatres, working so fast that he often reused his own music, overtures included. The comedies *L’italiana in Algeri*, *The Barber of Seville* (Rome, 1816; a failure on its first night, then a triumph) and *La Cenerentola* made his name across Europe, and serious operas such as *Tancredi* and *Semiramide* were just as admired. In 1822 he visited Vienna, where his operas caused a craze, and met Beethoven. Two years later he moved to Paris, and there, in 1829, he wrote *Guillaume Tell*, his last opera.

He then stopped writing operas, at thirty-seven, for reasons that have never been fully explained: ill health, wealth, and a change in taste towards grand spectacle may all have played a part. He went on composing in private: a *Stabat Mater*, songs, and more than 150 small pieces he called “sins of old age”, many written for the Saturday salons he held at his villa in Passy, where Liszt and Verdi were among the guests. His last large work was the *Petite messe solennelle*. He died at Passy in 1868; in 1887 his remains were moved to Santa Croce in Florence.
birthdayNote: Rossini was born on 29 February, so the real birthday comes round only once every four years. In other years we celebrate a day early, with the gallop that ends the *William Tell* Overture.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1792, in Pesaro.

name: Camille Saint-Saëns

facts.label: bestKnownFor
facts.value: *The Carnival of the Animals*, *Danse macabre*, *Samson and Delilah*

bio:
Saint-Saëns was born in Paris in 1835. His father, an official at the Ministry of the Interior, died of tuberculosis when Camille was only a few months old, and the boy was brought up by his mother and her aunt, Charlotte Masson, who taught him the piano. Before he was three he showed perfect pitch, and at ten, in 1846, he made his official debut at the Salle Pleyel, playing concertos by Mozart and Beethoven. At thirteen he entered the Paris Conservatoire, where he studied the organ with François Benoist and composition with Fromental Halévy. He was just as gifted at school, and kept a lifelong amateur passion for astronomy.

In 1853 he became organist of the church of Saint-Merri, and in 1858 of La Madeleine, the official church of the Empire; Liszt heard him there and called him the greatest organist in the world. From 1861 to 1865 he taught the piano at the École Niedermeyer, where his pupil Gabriel Fauré became a friend for life. In 1871, after the Franco-Prussian War, he helped to found the Société nationale de musique to promote new French music. He admired Liszt’s [[symphonic-poem|symphonic poem]]s and wrote his own, among them *Danse macabre*, and it was through Liszt that his opera *Samson and Delilah* was first staged, at Weimar in 1877. His marriage of 1875 collapsed after both his young sons died in 1878; he left his wife in 1881.

By the 1880s he was famous across Europe, especially in England, where the Philharmonic Society of London commissioned his “Organ” Symphony in 1886. That year he also finished *The Carnival of the Animals*, but forbade performances of it in his lifetime, fearing it would harm his name as a serious composer. He travelled constantly, wintered in Algiers and Egypt, and in 1908 wrote a score for the film *L’Assassinat du duc de Guise*. In old age he attacked Debussy and the new music of the 20th century, and came to be seen as a conservative. He died in Algiers in December 1921, aged 86, and was given a state funeral at the Madeleine. He once wrote that art exists to create beauty and character, and that feeling comes afterwards; Fauré and Fauré’s pupil Ravel revered him as a genius.
birthdayNote: In *Danse macabre* Death plays a violin with its top string tuned down, so the open strings clash. The skeletons dance until a cockerel, played by the oboe, sends them back to their graves.

name: Franz Schubert
bio:
Schubert was born in Vienna in 1797, the son of a schoolmaster. As a boy he sang in the choir of the imperial court chapel, which came with a place at a boarding school, where he played in the student orchestra and had lessons with Antonio Salieri. For a few years he taught at his father’s school, but what he really did was write music, at an astonishing rate.

He never held an important post, and he was never famous in the way Beethoven was, though they lived in the same city. Instead he had a devoted circle of friends, who gathered for evenings of his music that came to be called Schubertiades. He wrote more than 600 songs, among them *Erlkönig*, composed when he was 18, and the song cycle *Winterreise* (“Winter Journey”).

He fell seriously ill in his mid-twenties and died in 1828, aged just 31. Much of his greatest music, including the *Unfinished* Symphony and the *Great* C major Symphony, was only performed in public years after his death. His gift was melody, but also mood: in Schubert, a sudden change of key can feel like a cloud passing over the sun.
birthdayNote: Schubert’s friends used the nickname “Schwammerl”, little mushroom, and gathered for evenings of the composer’s music that they called Schubertiades. Today is a good day for one.
birthdayLine: Born on this day in 1797, in Vienna.
